clue.text: Golden bells?

parts.note: two hoops of gold exchanged at a marriage, read as if they were peals rung from a church tower on the day

explanation.surface: A pair of bells cast in gold.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is on 'rings': the bands are golden, and church bells ring at a marriage, so both words of the clue point at the same pair of objects.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain gold bands are what a couple exchange in the marriage ceremony.

clue.text: Today's Engagements? Say that again, my boy

parts.note: a puzzled 'What?' asks the speaker to repeat themselves
a parent's boy is a son

explanation.surface: A parent, half-listening to the day's diary, asks the child to repeat it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What, son?' is how a deaf father might say 'Say that again, my boy'; run together it becomes the newspaper heading for the day's events.
explanation.definitionFit: A listings column of shows and events happening today carries this heading.

clue.text: Lets the sweeties fall

parts.note: letting things fall is one sense of the word, and fruit-flavoured boiled sweets carry the same name, so the clue describes letting sweets slip

explanation.surface: A child lets a bag of sweets spill onto the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb meaning 'lets fall' is also the name of small boiled sweets (fruit drops, acid drops), so the clue reads two ways at once.
explanation.definitionFit: To let something fall is to release it, and small round boiled confections share that name.

clue.text: Characteristic of Mum in such a foolish situation

indicators.note: Mum is placed inside the foolish word, as the clue says she is in that situation

parts.note: a foolish, absurd state of affairs is idiotic
Mum is another word for mother, ma

explanation.surface: A mother finds herself in an embarrassingly silly predicament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characteristic' here means typical of a language's natural usage; 'situation' only dresses the foolish word, and 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An expression true to the natural usage peculiar to a language is said to be typical of it.

clue.text: God-appointed situation of Mrs. Alexander's poor man

definitions.text: God-appointed situation of Mrs. Alexander's poor man

parts.words: God-appointed situation of Mrs. Alexander's poor man
parts.note: the hymn verse says the rich man sits in his castle and the poor man stands at his entrance, as God ordered their estate

explanation.surface: A question about where a hymn places the poor man in God's order.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Cecil Frances Alexander wrote the hymn 'All Things Bright and Beautiful', whose once-familiar verse runs 'The rich man in his castle, The poor man at his ___, God made them high or lowly, And ordered their estate.'
explanation.definitionFit: The hymn stations the poor man at the entrance to the rich man's grounds.

clue.text: Can't I hoe here? Just begun

indicators.note: the question asks whether ground can be worked over at this spot, and the letters before it are worked over into a new order

explanation.surface: A gardener, barely started, asks whether this plot can be hoed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'here' signals the anagram: CANT I HOE rearranges to the answer. The apostrophe in 'Can't' gives no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in an undeveloped, rudimentary state has only started to take shape.

clue.text: Overhead transport for American infantry

parts.note: GI is the term for an American soldier, especially an infantryman
a bus is a form of public transport

explanation.surface: A request for buses to carry American soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overhead' is the definition as a noun: something worn over the head. The GIBUS is a collapsible opera hat, named after its French inventor.
explanation.definitionFit: A collapsible silk top hat is headgear, a thing worn on top of the head.

clue.text: Is denial a form of madness ?

parts.note: French démenti, used in English for an official contradiction of a report, means a denial

explanation.surface: A psychological question: is refusing to accept the truth a kind of insanity?
explanation.walkthrough: A DEMENTI (from French) is an official denial of a rumour; add A. 'Is' is a link word, and the question mark covers the borrowed word.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a chronic decline of mental faculties, long used loosely for insanity.

clue.text: Time for a water-baby ?

parts.note: the sea is a body of water
a baby boy is someone's son

explanation.surface: An allusion to Kingsley's children's story The Water-Babies, asking when one is due.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated 'water-baby' recalls Charles Kingsley's novel The Water-Babies, but it splits into two plain words; 'for a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A period of the year, such as summer, is a span of time.

clue.text: Samson's athletic appearance

parts.note: Milton's dramatic poem about Samson takes a Greek word for a contestant as its title, and its adjective means combative or athletic

explanation.surface: A remark on how the strongman Samson looked.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's poem is 'Samson Agonistes', Samson the champion or wrestler; the related adjective means athletic or combative, so the clue joins the title and the sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes contests of strength, from Greek agon, an athletic contest.

clue.text: A note from the Vatican

parts.note: the word is both a long musical note and a short papal letter, so a note from the Pope fits both readings

explanation.surface: The Pope sends a short letter.
explanation.walkthrough: A breve is a papal brief, less formal than a bull, and also a musical note worth two semibreves; the clue's 'note' covers both.
explanation.definitionFit: It names both a papal letter of lesser solemnity than a bull and a long musical time value.

clue.text: Seedy sort of door-opener

definitions.meaning: a plant grown for its small oily seeds, seedy in the literal sense
the password in Ali Baba that makes the robbers' cave door open

explanation.surface: A disreputable type who lets people in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seedy' suggests shabby, but here it means bearing seeds; 'Open ___!' is Ali Baba's magic command.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant yields edible seeds, and its name is the magic word in the Arabian Nights tale that opens a cave.

clue.text: I'm among rich tapestries getting briefs

indicators.note: the speaker says they are among the hangings, so the letter for 'I' goes inside them

parts.note: a dosser (or dorser) is an ornamental cloth hung at the back of a seat or altar
I'm is I am, the speaker, giving I

explanation.surface: Someone surrounded by sumptuous wall-hangings receives instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' puts I inside DOSSERS, old rich hangings for the back of a seat. 'Briefs' are not underwear but sets of documents.
explanation.definitionFit: A file of papers on a case or person is a set of written instructions or background, like a lawyer's case papers.

clue.text: Dark components of poetic chequer-board

parts.note: FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam calls life a chequer-board of alternating dark and light squares, the dark ones being the hours after sunset

explanation.surface: A question about the black squares of a chessboard in a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rubaiyat line is 'Tis all a Chequer-board of Nights and Days'; the dark squares are the dark half.
explanation.definitionFit: Periods of darkness are the black squares set against days in the poem's image.

clue.text: In which Ruth might have posed for Millet?

definitions.text: In which Ruth might have posed for Millet?

parts.words: In which Ruth might have posed for Millet
parts.note: Millet painted peasant women picking up leftover grain in a field, which is exactly what the biblical Ruth did in Boaz's field

explanation.surface: A question about which painting the biblical Ruth could have modelled for.
explanation.walkthrough: Millet's famous 1857 painting shows three women gathering stray ears of wheat after the harvest; in the Book of Ruth, Ruth gathers grain in the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: Women who gather leftover grain after reapers are the subject of Millet's best-known canvas.

clue.text: Supply fashion in original railway town

parts.note: a supply or store of goods is stock
ton is an old word for fashion or the fashionable world, as in 'bon ton'

explanation.surface: A trader supplying fashions in a historic railway town.
explanation.walkthrough: The Stockton and Darlington Railway of 1825 was the first public steam railway; Stockton-on-Tees is a town in north-east England. 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Teesside town was one end of the world's first passenger steam railway line.

clue.text: With a goat Circe makes an absolute transformation

indicators.note: Circe turned men into beasts, and here the letters of the goat and her name are turned into something else

explanation.surface: The sorceress Circe performs a complete metamorphosis with a goat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transformation' signals the anagram of GOAT CIRCE; in the Odyssey Circe transforms men into animals, which makes the surface fit.
explanation.definitionFit: An unconditional, unqualified statement is described this way.

clue.text: Pressure in the time of Charles O'Malley's creator?

parts.note: the Irish novelist Charles Lever wrote 'Charles O'Malley, the Irish Dragoon' (1841)
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Asking about pressure in the days of a Victorian novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the time of' the author is his age, so LEVER + AGE; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Leverage is the power to influence or push someone, figurative force applied.

clue.text: Digger's a hungry man !

parts.note: one who digs ditches has the same name as a wooden platter, and a hearty eater is a good man at that platter

explanation.surface: A labourer who digs is always ravenous.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means a trench-digger and also a wooden plate; a hearty eater is a 'good trencherman', so the digger and the hungry man share the name.
explanation.definitionFit: It means a ditch-digger and, through the trencher plate, someone who eats heartily.

clue.text: Blasted good fellows!

parts.note: the word means blasts on a trumpet and also, in old slang, fine dependable fellows

explanation.surface: An exclamation of grudging praise for some decent chaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blasted' looks like a mild oath, but it hints at trumpet blasts; a 'trump' was also slang for a splendid person, so the plural covers both.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang calls a reliable, generous person a trump, and the word also means trumpet blasts.

clue.text: Hats for Stalky and Co. ?

parts.note: Kipling's schoolboys in 'Stalky and Co.' wore boaters, hats woven from dried stalks

explanation.surface: Asking what headgear Kipling's schoolboy heroes wore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stalky and Co.' is Kipling's story of three boys at an English boarding school, where flat stiff summer hats were standard; 'Stalky' hints at stalks, the hats' material.
explanation.definitionFit: Boaters woven from dried cereal stalks were school headgear.

clue.text: Warning leg pressure results in a row

parts.note: the shin is the front of the lower leg
a dig is a sharp jab or poke

explanation.surface: A warning kick under the table leads to an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warning' only colours the picture: a dig on the shin is a warning nudge. 'results in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A noisy party or a disturbance can both be a commotion, a row in the sense of a rumpus.

clue.text: In a word, "See my courage 'is out "

definitions.text: In a word, "See my courage 'is out "

parts.words: In a word, "See my courage 'is out
parts.note: a stage character complaining that his nerve has gone, summed up in a single word

explanation.surface: A frightened speaker announces that his courage has left him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a word' asks for one word summing up the quotation: someone whose nerve has gone out of him has been deprived of nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: Having lost one's nerve or courage is the plain sense of the word.

clue.text: The mount of poetry

parts.note: Wordsworth's later home in the Lake District was a house called Mount, after the hill beside it

explanation.surface: A reference to a poetic mountain, like Parnassus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' suggests Parnassus, the Greek mountain of poetry, but it is Rydal Mount, Wordsworth's house near Ambleside in the English Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth lived at Rydal Mount from 1813 until his death.

clue.text: Guinea-pig type gets Lloyd's approval without relish

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the approval mark goes round the relish

parts.note: A1 is the top rating in Lloyd's Register of ships, read as letters A I
goût, French for taste, is used in English for relish or liking

explanation.surface: A rodent passes inspection but has no appetite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, so A1 wraps GOUT; the 1 serves as the letter I. The agouti is a South American rodent related to the guinea pig.
explanation.definitionFit: The agouti is a cavy-like rodent, close kin to the guinea pig.

clue.text: From a Russian mountain I get the curare plant

parts.note: the Urals are the mountain range dividing European and Asian Russia

explanation.surface: A botanist collects a poison plant from Russian mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: URAL is a mountain of the Urals; add I. 'From' and 'get' are links. Urali is a variant name of curare, the arrow poison.
explanation.definitionFit: Urali is another name for the South American arrow-poison plant and its extract.

clue.text: "The angry — doth glow on Caesar's brow " (J. Caesar)

definitions.text: "The angry — doth glow on Caesar's brow " (J. Caesar)

parts.words: The angry — doth glow on Caesar's brow
parts.note: Brutus, in Act 1 Scene 2 of Julius Caesar, describes a red mark of anger on Caesar's forehead, and the missing word names that mark

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Julius Caesar with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the gap in the quotation: Brutus says 'The angry ___ doth glow on Caesar's brow'.
explanation.definitionFit: A small coloured mark or blotch on the skin is the word Shakespeare used.

clue.text: Sire with revolutionary tinge is well shaved

parts.note: a sire is a father, pa
red is the colour of revolution

explanation.surface: A father with a tint of red is cleanly shaven.
explanation.walkthrough: PA (father) plus RED (the colour of revolutionaries); 'with' and 'is' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Something trimmed close, cut down to the skin, has been shaved closely.

clue.text: The mark of more to come

definitions.text: The mark of more to come

parts.words: The mark of more to come
parts.note: the symbol written for 'and', which promises something further is to follow

explanation.surface: A sign that more is on its way.
explanation.walkthrough: The '&' sign stands for 'and', which always leads on to something more.
explanation.definitionFit: The '&' symbol is the written sign for 'and'.

clue.text: Vesey and Montagu for hose

parts.note: Elizabeth Vesey and Elizabeth Montagu hosted the 18th-century literary salons whose informal dress gave learned women their nickname, which also names coloured hosiery

explanation.surface: Two society ladies are chosen for stockings.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Vesey and Mrs Montagu ran London literary gatherings where a guest wore blue worsted stockings, so learned women became 'bluestockings'; 'hose' points at the stocking itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A learned or literary woman was nicknamed after the coloured hosiery at those salons.
